title: joan fontcuberta's landscapes remapping photography and the technological image
display_name: JOAN FONTCUBERTA'S LANDSCAPES — REMAPPING PHOTOGRAPHY AND THE TECHNOLOGICAL IMAGE
abstract: click to increase image sizeclick to decrease image size acknowledgements i would like to thank joan fontcuberta for granting me permission to reproduce several of his images here. not only has his work provided a tremendous source of pleasure and intellectual engagement for me over the past years, but his generosity and openly collaborative spirit have been extremely helpful and very much appreciated. notes 1. see introduction to cosgrove. 2. costelaciones, hemogramas, semi polis are three separate photographic projects by fontcuberta, all collected together in one volume published in 2000 by actar, madrid, under the title zonas de penumbra (twilight zones). 3. it should be noted here that this intertwining of real and imaginary is also an integral part of much of fontcuberta's earlier works, particularly those dating from the 1980s and 90s, where ostensibly everyday objects (animals, plants, etc.) or ordinary spaces (backyards, parks, home interiors, etc.) take on uncanny qualities, appearing as something other than what they actually are, or vice versa. often interrogating scientific objectivity by drawing on ironic forms of naming and classifying, his works play with the act of observation and call into question the process of perception. for instance, the photographic collection titled herbarium (1982 85), in which fontcuberta creates imaginary plants from real materials, could easily be identified as a project that anticipates the artist's later work on imaginary places and invented or false landscapes, as i have been discussing up until this point. one of the more intriguing examples from the herbarium series is guillumeta polipodida (1982) the viewer is presented with an exquisite, highly formalist black and white photograph of a plant, catalogued in the series according to its pseudo-scientific but ultimately invented name (the photograph's title). upon close inspection, the viewer notices that the organic folds and naturalist contours of the plant, though seemingly lifelike, are composed of industrial waste. fontcuberta incorporates these playful turns, ironic bricolages, and processes of conversion in, among other examples, his photographs detailing specimens from natural history museums and, perhaps more notably still, his early work titled fauna, in which he documents the rediscovery (and subsequent exhibition and archivization) of non-existent animals such as the alopex stultus (1986), a tortoise with long legs and a fur coat. here, of course, my analysis covers only his more recent works from the late 1990s and 2000s, though in large part the same theoretical underpinnings are present in these earlier collections, which do deserve further attention. for a complete listing of fontcuberta's early works, visit http://www.fontcuberta.comfor a very brief yet well-done introduction to select early works, see joan fontcuberta from phaidon press published in 2001. 4. for reasons of time and space, i have limited my theoretical approach to those critics and scholars who are specifically interested in the image as either a site of production, a structure of knowledge, or a filter of visible and invisible information. this is one reason why i draw on certain arguments outlined by benjamin and cadava, to name only two examples. however, i would also like to make mention here of another theoretical framework the derridean one that i do not explicitly draw on though it has discernible connections with my readings and therefore could be discussed quite productively in concert with fontcuberta's work, and more specifically with the artist's explorations of archival logic, a point i will discuss in section ii of this essay. this, of course, is not to dismiss or exclude any valuable insights that such connections could bear, but rather to acknowledge them here as such, even though they would need (and deserve) proper attention in a separate essay. that said, among the many relevant arguments that derrida's thinking may contribute to any reading of fontcuberta's photography, one in particular stands out. this is none other than the re-conceptualization in archive fever of the archive not as a place of consignment or of the past per se, but rather as a question of the future, the question of the future itself, the question of a response, of a promise and of a responsibility for tomorrow (derrida 36). i have written about this connection elsewhere (in an unpublished piece titled joan fontcuberta's googlegrams and the virtual archive ) and simply wish to note here that derrida's rethinking of the archive as a place of invention and forgetting, as opposed to truth and memory, along with his examination of the archive's tendency towards futurity rather than what t.s. eliot calls the pastness of the past are worthy grounds for future exploration in another essay. 5. for complete artist's statement, see zabriskie gallery website: http://www.zabriskiegallery.com/artist.php?artist=5&page=45. 6. from the university of nottingham's lakeside arts exhibition notes titled joan fontcuberta, datascapes . http://www.lakesidearts.org.uk/exhibitions/viewevent.html?e=1336&c=5&d=0 7. from nuevas historias site: http://nuevashistorias.com/index/intro/fontcuberta/ 8. zabriskie gallery online does an excellent job of displaying two views of each googlegram the first is the entire photograph; the second is a fragment which details an enlarged section of the photograph, magnifying the hyper-pixelated quality of individual tiles. this twin view is helpful for understanding how these photographs appear at a distance versus how they look up close. however, exhibitions of the googlegrams have typically not included multiple views but have occasionally included a list of the search words used. 9. this forms part of enwezor's engaging reading of jef geys's work in a section of his essay titled archives as meditations on time . see pages 23 26 of the same essay. 10. i would like to thank kurt buhanan (uc irvine) for a helpful comment about multi-stable images made in relation to a paper i gave on joan fontcuberta's googlegrams at the csulb 45th annual comparative literature conference visual culture and global practices . this comment led me to explore some of the ideas laid out in w.j.t. mitchell's picture theory, in which he considers different kinds of dialectical images whose primary function is to illustrate the co-existence of contrary or simply different readings in the single image, a phenomenon sometimes called multi-stability (45). this is a fascinating point and clearly overlaps with my own reading of fontcuberta's work, insofar as multi-stability operates on ambiguity, or the ambiguity of the image's boundaries, which results in the ambiguity of their referentiality (mitchell 48). i would argue that the googlegrams indeed are ambiguous in this sense. on a slightly different yet related note, one can imagine that any non-ambiguity would also, at least in part, depend on the distance between observer and photograph. distance would, at least in theory, allow one to focus more easily on the larger iconic figure, whereas proximity would enhance the visibility and non-ambiguity of the individual tiles. 11. the following is an excerpt from the artist's statement from the zabriskie gallery website (cited above): in my previous work the archive has been a recurring presence. on numerous occasions i have used the faked discovery of an archive as the starting point for a critique, parody and deconstruction of the whole concept of the document. on other occasions i have looked at issues of representation, focusing, for example, on the notion of the palimpsest. googlegrams combines the two strategies. the basic idea consists in selecting images that have become icons of our time. for example, one of the widely disseminated photos of the torture scandal in the abu ghraib prison in baghdad: private lynndie r. england holding a leash tied around the neck of a prisoner as if he were a dog. in one googlegram this photograph has been refashioned using a freeware photo mosaic programme. the photo mosaic is a technique used by graphic designers and photo enthusiasts that consists in composing an image out of a large number of tiny images, which function like the cells in a reticular structure. the programme selects each graphic sample from the bank of available images and places it according to chromatic value and density in the position that most closely coincides with a portion of the larger image being recreated, as if it were making a gigantic jigsaw puzzle. logically, the greater the number of cells, the sharper the resulting image will be. [paragraph break] for the googlegrams, however, the programme was connected to the internet and used the search engine google to locate thousands of images on the basis of search criteria determined by the user, normally images associated with one or several words. in the abu ghraib photograph, for example, the search engine was given the names of top officials, civilian contractors and enlisted soldiers cited in the final report of the independent panel to review dod detention operations (august 2004) of the schlesinger panel, set up by the united states congress to investigate the alleged abuses. 12. see walter benjamin ( little history , a short history ). the notion of image worlds seems to directly contest sontag's understanding of photography in in plato's cave (on photography), when she writes to collect photographs is to collect the world (8). see also sabine t. kriebel. 13. one could even take this reading of the googlegrams underlying multiplicity (always working against the grain of singularity ) one step further to draw a parallel between fontcuberta's photographs of photographs or images of images and the internet itself, which is, by definition, a massive network of networks . 14. departing from benjamin's ideas, the googlegrams also signal the passing of time as an embedded problem in each photograph (this will be discussed later in the paper). in other words, they are of particular interest since they play on the notion of arrest the benjaminian flash or fragment and flows, movement, and the future perhaps a wink at marx's locomotive of history , which in a large sense is pitted against benjamin's understanding of history. see cadava's introduction in words of light. 15. of course, one could argue that this is the case in all art, and especially conceptual art that our reading changes over time. fontcuberta really drives this point home by making it, i argue, the central component of his work. 16. see zabriskie gallery exhibitions artist's notes, titled archival noise, written by joan fontcuberta. http://www.zabriskiegallery.com/exhibition.php?ex=13&page=45 http://www.zabriskiegallery.com/exhibition.php?ex=13&page=45 http://www.zabriskiegallery.com/exhibition.php?ex=13&page=45 17. see zabriskie gallery notes. ibid. 18. from the zabriskie gallery notes. ibid. 19. from the zabriskie gallery notes. ibid. 20. from the zabriskie gallery notes. ibid. 21. though it falls out of the scope of the present essay, it certainly would be worthwhile to trace the concept of the archive in several other projects from fontcuberta's corpus, including his early photography, as briefly noted above. in terms of placing the archive in relation to forgetting and structures of erasure (rather than, for instance, memory and structures of remembrance), it would be interesting to examine how his imitation (and debunking) of scientific photography as documentary evidence and accurate method of historical and anthropological archiving calls into question not only the medium's objectivity , but also, and more crucially, its ability to empty objects of meaning, resulting in our inability to ever access the past or approach any notion of historical truth since our own perceptions, like the photographs we study, are always constructed, mediated and subjective. 22. i would like to thank the students from my spanish 4750 course, landscapes and loss: visualizing contemporary spain , at cornell university (fall 2009), for their comments and questions on joan fontcuberta's method. the students were primarily (and rightly) interested in the question of perspective and subjectivity whether the artist chose the perspective, say, that one might choose when looking through a normal viewer finder of a camera. this was part of our discussion about the nature and place of the artist in taking the photograph. i countered with a different example: robert frank, who, as many know, rarely ever looked through the viewfinder, opting instead to find views from elsewhere. regardless, i think the point my students raised was indeed an interesting one. after all, it is fontcuberta who decides which painting the computer will scan. how does it change our reading of the computer's reading of a given painting, if he also chooses a specific perspective or setting (out of several, we can assume)? there is a kind of double intervention on the part of the artist, in my opinion. fontcuberta says that using the default setting was his original idea, which the artist claims was conceptually very strong, but visually very boring. i changes [sic] and tried to do interventions in the settings marine landscapes, cliffs, islands, etc. i was trying to present an inventory. finally the result was a little kitsch-y. amazingly the program tends to duplicate reality automatically. i was trying to represent different models that we can find in the history [sic] landscape painting. the mountain landscape, the desert, the misty valley (fontcuberta, http://www.nottinghamvisualarts.net/review/apr-09/hitchhikers-guide-gallery)

title: the revival of the historic islamic geometric pattern on the gate of the al-sharabeya school in wasit city using the grasshopper program
display_name: The revival of the historic Islamic geometric pattern on the gate of The Al-Sharabeya School in Wasit City using the Grasshopper program
abstract: there is a lack of knowledge that is required for using computer programs (parametric computing) to generate and derive new islamic geometric patterns locally. this study focuses on the application of parametric modeling using the rhinoceros 6 grasshopper program on an islamic geometric historical pattern, which decorated the gate of the school in wasit, where the search imposes a spatial approach. this program is applied with the help of the algorithmic parameters used by the parametric design technique to generate and derive new islamic geometric patterns from an extinct reference pattern used in contemporary urbanism. the goal is to enhance and impart an attribute of cultural inclusion and architectural originality to the local architecture of cities. the results demonstrate that the program was able to generate a new islamic geometric pattern that did not previously exist, by finding the associative relationships and a hidden network between the tessellations of the islamic geometric pattern, through algorithmic relationships, which was not visible. therefore, the rhinoceros 6 grasshopper program can be used by architects and urbanites to devise distinctive design alternatives based on historical patterns and heritage models that can be applied in the future design of urban areas and cities that belong to the islamic civilization.
